source.title: Understanding the Repeat Curse in Large Language Models from a Feature Perspective
source.authors: Jun-Chi Yao; Shu Yang; Jianhua Xu; Lijie Hu; Mengdi Li; Di Wang

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether SAE-derived features in LLMs can be identified and causally manipulated, bearing on V4’s claim that dictionaries can recover sparse features. It does not measure superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The study reports SAE-feature activation and deactivation results. Table 1’s RF and common-feature comparisons are included; intermediate activation ratios are omitted due to the row limit. The Table 2 comparison of the paper’s mitigation method with decoding methods is not a result about SAE features themselves. Layer-attribution results guide layer selection and are not included as feature-recovery outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained SAEs as a tool to find and steer 'repetition features' and reports the effect of its own pipeline (DUC) on repeat scores. It does not test whether LLMs hold features in superposition or whether SAEs recover the model's features. No reconstruction quality, no neuron-vs-feature comparison, no geometry. Repetition features are defined as those whose activation yields RS ≥ 0.4, and common features as RS < 0.4. The RF-vs-CF contrast in Table 1 therefore follows from the selection rule and does not independently test V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors claim SAE 'repetition features' (chosen by repeat score ≥ 0.4 after steering) induce repetition when activated. They say deactivating them mitigates repetition, but mainly on EQ; AQ and NQ show only minor fluctuations. They report no significant perplexity cost and say repetition features cluster around names, time and mathematics.
record.recipe_differences: Uses pretrained SAEs and activation steering to identify and manipulate repetition-related features in LLMs; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition method or measure feature-direction geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported repeat scores vary with model, layer, dataset, and activation ratio. Authors state that EQ shows the clearest deactivation response and that GPT2-small is more sensitive to repetition-feature activation than the larger tested models.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering selected SAE latents in GPT2-small, Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.1-8B raises 1-gram repeat score, e.g. 0.37→0.72 (GPT2 L9, EQ). Turning them down lowers it mainly on EQ, e.g. 0.37→0.19.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents in LLMs causally control a specific generation behaviour (repetition) when steered.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Only three models with available pretrained SAEs are tested; the paper itself notes their relatively limited scale and open-source SAE availability. The feature-selection threshold is set to ρ = 0.4 based on human evaluation and is acknowledged as subjective. The reported Table 1 averages have no stated sample counts or uncertainty estimates. Repetition-feature behavior is identified through deliberate feature steering and repetition-oriented prompts, so the results do not establish how often these features produce repetition without intervention.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 results at activation ratios 20% and 50%, and the deactivation entries, are not extracted because of the 60-row limit; the kept rows retain the 10% and 100% activation endpoints for every model-layer-dataset combination and matched common-feature controls at 100%. The omitted entries are in Table 1. Table 13’s single-feature example and Appendix F’s human-evaluation examples are also not extracted.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All: no capacity or importance analysis.
All: no analysis of why neurons are polysemantic.
The study assumes, rather than tests, that SAEs recover the model's sparse features. There is no measure of feature spread across neurons and no reconstruction or recovery evaluation.
All: no completeness, stability or canonicity tests.
All: no comparison with multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is an application of pretrained SAEs to the repetition problem. It cites superposition only to motivate using SAEs. The RF/CF contrast is built into the feature-selection threshold, so it cannot serve as evidence that SAEs recover the model's features. The reader's V4 'supports' label is removed.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, feature overlap and orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Capacity competition, dedicated dimensions for important features, and sharing of dimensions by other features.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.

The study tests SAE feature identification and steering for repetition in three LLMs; it does not measure how broadly features are distributed across neurons, establish general recovery across tasks, or test other dictionary methods.
Feature completeness, stability, or canonical status is not evaluated.
No comparison of one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features, or direct measurement of feature geometry.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Repetition-feature activation in the reported GPT2-small, Gemma-2-2B, and Llama-3.1-8B settings, at 10% and 100% activation ratios, across EQ, AQ, and NQ
reader_labels.reason: Repeat scores rise from original values when SAE-identified repetition features are activated; the study reports no significant change for matched common-feature controls (r1-r36; r37-r54). This supports feature recoverability in these tested settings, not a general claim about all LLM features.
